# Software Architecture and Microservice Workshop

*Building effective software efficiently*

## Loosely Coupled Distributed Architecture

The cart service is currently tightly coupled to the catalogue service. Whenever
a user requests cart information or adds a new item, the cart service must
communicate directly with the catalogue service, as shown below:

![Read cart details distributed high coupling](./assets/images/Read%20cart%20details%20distributed%20high%20coupling.png)

This tight coupling is not ideal. As mentioned earlier, we have inherited the
complexities of a distributed system without realising many of its benefits.

We can reduce this coupling by introducing a message queue. With this approach,
the catalogue service will publish an event each time a new catalogue item is
added. The cart service will consume these events and update its own copy of the
catalogue items in a local table. Yes—that means creating a new table in the
cart service to hold catalogue item data.

![Add new catalogue item distributed loosely coupled](./assets/images/Add%20new%20catalogue%20item%20distributed%20loosely%20coupled.png)

The cart service can then join against this local table whenever it needs
catalogue item data, avoiding synchronous REST calls to the catalogue service.

![Read cart details distributed loosely coupled](./assets/images/Read%20cart%20details%20distributed%20loosely%20coupled.png)

This approach simplifies cart and catalogue lookups, but it also shifts
complexity elsewhere. As you will see, there is no such thing as a free lunch:
every design choice has trade-offs, and it is not always obvious upfront which
ones will pay off.

There are several widely used messaging queues available, including
[RabbitMQ](https://www.rabbitmq.com/) and
[ActiveMQ](https://activemq.apache.org/). For this example, we will use
RabbitMQ, as it currently trends more strongly according to
[Google Trends](https://trends.google.com/trends/explore?cat=32&q=RabbitMQ,ActiveMQ&hl=en-US).
Popularity does not necessarily mean a better product, but it often means more
examples, documentation, and community support. In practice, the more a
technology is used and tested, the less likely we are to encounter unforeseen
issues.

### Architecture Decision Records (ADR)

Another architectural decision has been made to refactor the distributed
application, moving from synchronous to asynchronous communication. RabbitMQ was
chosen over ActiveMQ due to its greater popularity and strong, active community
support. This refactoring will remove the dependency of the cart service on the
catalogue service. Once complete, the cart service will be able to function even
if the catalogue service is not running.

`ADR-008` has now been superseded with `ADR-011`, and thus it needs to be updated.

Lastly, update the `README.md` file, which summarises all ADRs, to include the
new ADR.

### A new approach

Synchronous communication, such as REST, closely resembles method calls and is
often referred to as remote procedure calls (RPC). Because of this similarity,
synchronous communication can be integrated easily into an existing flow:
instead of calling a local method, the cart service calls a remote one.

Asynchronous communication, however, works differently. Rather than the consumer
(e.g. the cart service) initiating a request, the producer emits events. In our
example, the catalogue service (the producer) will publish an event whenever a
new catalogue item is added. The cart service (the consumer) listens for these
events and records the new item when it arrives.

For this to work effectively, the cart service must maintain a local copy of all
catalogue items in its own database, updating it as new events are received.
This represents a significant change in flow: instead of the cart service
triggering requests, the catalogue service emits events as they occur.

In the synchronous approach, the cart service needed to know the location of the
catalogue service in order to send requests. In the asynchronous approach, a
message queue acts as a buffer between the two services, as shown below:

![Add new catalogue item distributed loosely coupled](./assets/images/Add%20new%20catalogue%20item%20distributed%20loosely%20coupled.png)

This diagram illustrates the new flow when a catalogue item is added.

This approach offers several advantages, including a reduction in direct
communication between services. It also shifts the dependency: the cart service
no longer depends directly on the catalogue service but instead depends on the
message queue. Both services now rely on the message queue as the intermediary.

The catalogue will publish an event each time a new item is added. The event’s
payload will contain the details of the new catalogue item in JSON format. JSON
was selected for its simplicity and portability. While other serialization
frameworks, such as [AVRO](https://avro.apache.org/) or
[Protobuf](https://protobuf.dev/), are available, I chose straightforward JSON
to maintain simplicity.

> **What are some of the considerations when selecting a serialization framework?**
>
> This is an important question. Serialization is a critical aspect of the API,
> as it defines how data is exchanged with the service. Different serialization
> frameworks offer distinct trade-offs.
>
> JSON, which we have chosen, is very straightforward to use; however, it is
> relatively inefficient in terms of data size. As we are exchanging only a few
> small messages, this inefficiency is not a concern in our case.
>
> In a typical production environment, significantly more messages may be
> exchanged, including those with large payloads. Here, message size becomes a
> key consideration. Both AVRO and Protobuf are binary protocols, meaning that
> they efficiently compress data and eliminate redundant fields. This makes them
> well suited to applications that handle a large volume of messages.
> Additionally, both frameworks support schema versioning, which, while
> advantageous, can introduce complications if not managed carefully.
>
> Despite these benefits, it is important to note that implementing either
> framework adds to the complexity of the overall setup.

> **Can we use Java serialisation instead?**
>
> Yes, it is possible. The message payload is a byte array, so anything that can
> be serialised into a `byte[]` is supported. However, it is important to note
> that using Java serialisation binds both the producer and consumer to the
> Java programming language. The same Java classes being serialised must also be
> available to both the producer (in this case, the catalogue service) and the
> consumer (the cart service).
>
> Although Java serialisation can be efficient, its use is generally discouraged
> due to security concerns. In his book
> [*Effective Java*](https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/effective-java-3rd/9780134686097/ch12.xhtml),
> Joshua Bloch highlights the vulnerabilities inherent in Java’s serialisation
> mechanism. He explains that deserialising untrusted data may expose
> applications to remote code execution, denial-of-service attacks, and other
> exploits. Bloch advises against using Java serialisation in new systems and
> recommends alternatives such as JSON or Protocol Buffers for data
> representation. He also stresses the need for caution when implementing
> `Serializable`, as it can limit flexibility in future class modifications and
> increase the risk of security issues.

When a new item is added to the catalogue, a message must be published to the
message queue (the `demo-exchange` exchange, using `demo.catalogue.new` as its
routing key) after it has been inserted into the catalogue table. The service
layer should perform two actions: invoke the `CatalogueItemRepository` to save
the item, and then publish the message.

> **Why is a new gateway needed to publish messages to the queue?**
>
> Introducing a gateway simplifies testing. For example, if we want to verify
> that the service only publishes a message after a successful database save
> operation, both the repository and the gateway can be mocked. This allows us
> to simulate different scenarios and assert the correct behaviour.
>
> Additionally, the gateway acts as an anti-corruption layer between the message
> queue and the application. Message queue-specific classes remain encapsulated
> within the gateway, shielding the application from the implementation details
> of the message queue.

> **Why are we using integration tests instead of unit tests?**
>
> This particular test verifies the entire flow, giving us confidence that the
> application is properly configured and capable of both persisting a new item
> to the database and sending the appropriate message to the message queue.
> Although this is an integration test, it is not slow; in fact, it is
> sufficiently fast to be run as often as needed.
>
> The main drawback is that it requires a running instance of RabbitMQ, which
> can be inconvenient. [TestContainers](https://testcontainers.com/) can help
> address this by spinning up dependencies on demand, but since I cannot run
> TestContainers without [Docker Desktop](https://docs.docker.com/desktop/), I
> must ensure that RabbitMQ is running before executing the test.

> **Should we use more unit tests than integration tests?**
>
> The rationale for favouring unit tests is to minimise the total time required
> to run all tests. Integration tests are generally slower than unit tests,
> although this is not always the case. As a result, it is common practice to
> have more unit tests than integration tests.
>
> Unit tests have a narrow focus and, while they are fast, they offer limited
> assurance that the overall component operates as expected. For example, unit
> tests do not cover complete flows, such as adding a new catalogue item; they
> simply verify that certain parts behave as expected for given inputs.
>
> Integration tests, by contrast, have a broader scope and verify end-to-end
> flows. Because of this, they can be slower and more complex, but they provide
> greater assurance that the application works as a whole. A commonly cited
> disadvantage of integration tests is that, when they fail, it can be difficult
> to pinpoint the source of the issue. However, I believe this concern is often
> overstated. For example, in our scenario, if the repository fails to insert
> the item into the table, the database-related assertion will fail, clearly
> indicating a database problem; the same reasoning applies to the message
> queue.
>
> Since our integration tests run quickly, we enjoy the benefit of high
> confidence in our application’s behaviour without incurring the penalty of
> slow test execution.

> **Should we replace the unit tests with integration tests?**
>
> No.
>
> This question shifts the focus away from what truly matters. The specific type
> of test is less important than the confidence the tests provide and the time
> required to run them. Our goal should be to achieve high confidence in the
> application’s behaviour while minimising the time spent running tests.
>
> I typically begin with an integration test to cover the entire flow, as we
> have done here. However, different options or branches can make it difficult
> to create integration tests for every possible combination. In such cases,
> unit tests are valuable for covering these variations. For example, we can use
> a unit test to verify that the service only calls the gateway if the
> repository operation succeeds.
>
> Tests themselves introduce a form of coupling, which can make it harder to
> modify the application. Unit tests often result in tighter coupling compared
> to integration tests; for instance, changing an internal method signature may
> break related unit tests but will not affect integration tests. Over-testing
> can be counterproductive and may cause more harm than good. It is important
> not to add tests simply for the sake of testing, but rather to add confidence
> through selective and purposeful testing.

### Test the application

Our application has several dependencies, including Jaeger and RabbitMQ. Before
testing the application, ensure that these services are running.

Start the RabbitMQ service

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --detach \
  --name 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-messaging-queue' \
  --env RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_USER=demo \
  --env RABBITMQ_DEFAULT_PASS=a_RAND0M_and_S3CUR3_password \
  --publish 5672:5672 \
  --publish 15672:15672 \
  'docker.io/rabbitmq:4.2.0-management'

# Wait for RabbitMQ to start
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://127.0.0.1:15672/')" -eq '200' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

The catalogue service will send messages to RabbitMQ each time a new catalogue
item is created. The cart service, in turn, will listen for these messages. For
this setup, we need the following:

- **An exchange**: where the catalogue service will publish messages.
- **A queue**: from which the cart service will consume messages.
- **A binding**: to connect the exchange to the queue, ensuring messages sent by
  the catalogue service are delivered to the cart service.

There are several ways to configure this. The simplest approach is to run three
commands. While straightforward, this is not necessarily the best practice—I
generally prefer infrastructure as code. However, for the purposes of this
workshop, we will use the simpler method to keep the focus on the goals and
objectives.

Let’s create the exchange, queue, and binding before moving on.

```shell
# Create the exchange where the messages will be sent
docker exec 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-messaging-queue' \
  rabbitmqadmin --username='demo' --password='a_RAND0M_and_S3CUR3_password' declare exchange name='demo-exchange' type='topic'

# Create the queue from where the messages will be read
docker exec 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-messaging-queue' \
  rabbitmqadmin --username='demo' --password='a_RAND0M_and_S3CUR3_password' declare queue name='demo-queue'

# Bind the exchange with the queue so that the messages sent by the catalogue service can be read by the cart service
docker exec 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-messaging-queue' \
  rabbitmqadmin --username='demo' --password='a_RAND0M_and_S3CUR3_password' declare binding source='demo-exchange' destination='demo-queue' routing_key='demo.catalogue.new'
```

Access the RabbitMQ admin page at
[http://localhost:15672](http://localhost:15672) using the following
credentials:

| Property      | Value                          |
| ------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Username      | `demo`                         |
| Password      | `a_RAND0M_and_S3CUR3_password` |
| Exchange Name | `demo-exchange`                |
| Queue Name    | `demo-queue`                   |
| Routing Key   | `demo.catalogue.new`           |

Start Jaeger.

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --detach \
  --name 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-jaeger' \
  --env COLLECTOR_ZIPKIN_HOST_PORT=:9411 \
  --publish 4317:4317 \
  --publish 4318:4318 \
  --publish 9411:9411 \
  --publish 16686:16686 \
  'docker.io/jaegertracing/all-in-one:1.74.0'

# Wait for Jaeger to start
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:16686/search')" -eq '200' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

Build and test the application

```shell
./mvnw clean verify
```

Create the reverse proxy container

```shell
(
  cd 'reverse-proxy' &&
  docker build \
    --file 'Dockerfile' \
    --tag 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous:reverse-proxy' \
    --load \
    .
)
```

Start the reverse proxy on host port `8080`, mapped to port `80` inside the
container. This avoids requiring permission to bind a privileged host port.

```shell
docker run \
  --rm \
  --detach \
  --name 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-reverse-proxy' \
  --publish 8080:80 \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous:reverse-proxy'

# Wait for Nginx to start
# The reverse proxy is configured to only redirect to the cart and catalogue endpoints, thus any other requests will yield a 404
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/')" -eq '404' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

Copy both JAR files to the
`application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-reverse-proxy/target`
directory (for convenience), start both applications and make a few requests.
This generates the trace data and sends it to our Jaeger instance.

```shell
# Start the catalogue application in the background and wait for it to be ready
java -jar './catalogue/target/application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-catalogue-1.0.0.jar' > './catalogue/target/application.log' 2>&1 &

# Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
echo "$!" > './catalogue/target/application.pid'

# Wait for the application to start
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1')" -eq '200' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

```shell
# Start the cart application in the background and wait for it to be ready
CATALOGUE_ROOT_URI='http://localhost:8080/' \
  java -jar './cart/target/application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-cart-1.0.0.jar' > './cart/target/application.log' 2>&1 &

# Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
echo "$!" > './cart/target/application.pid'

# Wait for the application to start
until [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/cart/1')" -eq '200' ]; do sleep 1; done
```

Once both components are ready, we can add a new item and verify that it has
been added to both components.

```shell
# Save the response in a file as we will use it later on
curl --silent \
  -X POST 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"caption":"Green Plant","description":"Put a little life in your living room!!"}' \
  | jq \
  > new-catalogue-item.json

# Print the output
jq . new-catalogue-item.json
```

The response that was returned from the catalogue component

```json
{
  "id": 6,
  "caption": "Green Plant",
  "description": "Put a little life in your living room!!"
}
```

Fetch the cart and its items.

```shell
curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/cart/3' | jq
```

The current cart contents

```json
{
  "id": 3,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 4,
      "caption": "Mug",
      "quantity": 4
    }
  ]
}
```

Add the new item to the cart.

```shell
# Read the new item id obtained from the previous command
ITEM_ID="$(jq .id new-catalogue-item.json)"

# Add the new item to cart with id 3
curl --silent -X POST "http://localhost:8080/cart/3/item/${ITEM_ID}" | jq
```

The cart contents after adding the newly created catalogue item.

```json
{
  "id": 3,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 4,
      "caption": "Mug",
      "quantity": 4
    },
    {
      "id": 6,
      "caption": "Green Plant",
      "quantity": 1
    }
  ]
}
```

The newly created item is added to the cart successfully, indicating that both
components are communicating as expected.

Once you have completed your testing, stop the application and the additional
services.

```shell
kill "$(cat './catalogue/target/application.pid')"
kill "$(cat './cart/target/application.pid')"
docker stop 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-messaging-queue'
docker stop 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-reverse-proxy'
docker stop 'application-distributed-messaging-queue-asynchronous-jaeger'
```

### Tradeoffs

Adopting asynchronous, event-driven communication trades tight, request/response
coordination for looser coupling and resilience. Producers (e.g., catalogue)
publish events like `ItemUpdated`; consumers (e.g., cart) react whenever they
can. This decoupling absorbs traffic spikes and isolates failures—if catalogue
is down, cart can still serve from a local read model and process a backlog
later. You also gain independent deployability, smoother scaling, and natural
backpressure via queues. In short: fewer cascades, better elasticity, and
graceful degradation during incidents.

The price is eventual consistency and data duplication. Views must be rebuilt
from events and may be temporarily stale: cart might show an outdated
description until it receives the latest catalogue event, or fulfilment may
accept an order before inventory is fully synchronised. Architects need patterns
such as sagas with compensations, read-your-writes safeguards (e.g., verify at
checkout), and clear UX for “pending” states. You must embrace the reality of
at-least-once delivery—design idempotent consumers, include deduplication keys,
and manage ordering (typically per aggregate key) where it matters.

Complexity shifts to reliability and observability of messaging. Producers
should use a transactional outbox (write DB + event atomically) to avoid lost
messages; consumers should handle poison messages with dead-letter queues and
replay safely. Versioning becomes schema-first: adopt event contracts, a schema
registry, and compatibility rules (additive changes, new event types).
End-to-end insight requires correlation/causation ids, trace propagation through
message headers, and dashboards for lag, DLQ rate, and replay health; without
these, debugging “why didn’t fulfilment ship this order?” is slow and
frustrating.

Finally, there are organisational and operational trade-offs. You introduce a
new critical dependency (the broker), capacity planning for queues, and more
nuanced testing: consumer-driven contract tests, fixture-based replays, and
scenario drills (e.g., catalogue flood, cart catch-up). Cognitive load
rises—teams must understand idempotency, ordering, and compensation semantics.
Done well, event-driven architecture enables rapid, resilient evolution; done ad
hoc, it can devolve into temporal bugs, invisible coupling, and hard-to-trace
failures. The gain is real—but it requires disciplined patterns, tooling, and
team readiness.

In an event-driven design, services publish and subscribe to events. When the
catalogue emits an `ItemAdded` event, the cart consumes it to update its local
cache. This decoupling improves change failure rate (4/5), since the cart can
continue working with cached data even if the catalogue is temporarily
unavailable. It also boosts MTTR (4/5), as the system degrades gracefully and
can replay missed events once the issue is fixed.

Deployment frequency (4/5) remains high: services can be deployed independently,
with consumers handling old and new event versions in parallel. However, lead
time (3/5) is slowed by the need to evolve events carefully, ensuring backward
compatibility across multiple consumers (cart, catalogue, etc.).

The downside is cognitive load (2/5). Developers must handle eventual
consistency, idempotency, and dead-letter queues. For example, fulfilment might
process an order before the cart has updated stock from the catalogue, leading
to subtle bugs. This added complexity reduces satisfaction (3/5), even if the
architecture is powerful. Communication (4/5) is stronger, though, since clear
event contracts encourage domain-based collaboration between teams.

#### Distributed Transactions

Distributed transactions are mechanisms designed to extend the ACID (Atomicity,
Consistency, Isolation, Durability) guarantees across multiple services or
databases within a distributed system. Typically, these transactions coordinate
updates and operations spanning independent data stores or microservices,
ensuring that either all changes succeed together or none are applied. A common
protocol for managing distributed transactions is two-phase commit (2PC). In
2PC, the process is divided into two stages: during the first (prepare) phase,
each participating service votes on whether it can commit; if all agree, the
coordinator instructs all participants to commit during the second phase. If any
participant opts to abort, all services are instructed to roll back the
transaction, thus ensuring atomicity across distributed components.

Distributed transactions aim to extend ACID guarantees across multiple services
or databases; however, they introduce significant challenges. The most immediate
concern is increased latency and system fragility: coordinating 2PC or similar
protocols requires multiple round trips between services. For example, in an
e-commerce workflow involving cart, catalogue, and payment services, each
participant must prepare, lock resources, and subsequently commit. If any single
service is slow or unavailable, the entire transaction stalls, thereby degrading
the customer experience.

Resource contention is another issue. Locks are often held until the global
transaction completes, which typically takes much longer than a local operation.
For instance, reserving items in the catalogue during checkout may block stock
updates until both cart and payment services confirm. At scale, this can quickly
lead to deadlocks, timeouts, or bottlenecks, reducing system throughput and
compromising availability.

Handling failures is particularly complex in distributed systems. Partial
failures are common—one service may successfully commit while another times out.
Recovery logic in 2PC is notoriously intricate and may necessitate manual
intervention. Without careful design, such scenarios can leave the system in an
inconsistent state; for example, the customer might be charged by the payment
service, but the fulfilment service never creates the order because the
transaction coordinator failed mid-process.

A particularly problematic scenario arises if a failure occurs during the second
phase of a 2PC. By this stage, every participant (e.g., cart, catalogue,
payment) has confirmed in the prepare phase that it can commit. If the
coordinator or any service fails before broadcasting or completing the final
commit, some participants may proceed while others remain in a prepared but
uncommitted state. This can leave the system in a state of limbo: resources may
be locked, inventory reserved, or even payments processed, but the overall
transaction remains incomplete. Recovering from such a situation is complex and
error-prone—for example, the payment service may have taken funds while the
fulfilment service never dispatches the order. Without robust recovery
mechanisms and reconciliation processes, these inconsistencies can erode
customer trust and necessitate costly manual remediation.

Finally, distributed transactions contravene a key principle of microservices
architecture: loose coupling and service autonomy. They tightly couple services
at runtime, making each dependent on the availability of others. Rather than
benefiting from the resilience and independent deployability of distributed
systems, the architecture inherits the weaknesses of a monolith, compounded by
network unreliability. For this reason, architects frequently avoid distributed
transactions in favour of sagas, eventual consistency, and compensating actions.

#### BASE

In traditional monolithic systems, we rely on ACID transactions—Atomicity,
Consistency, Isolation, Durability—to guarantee correctness. For example, when a
customer checks out their cart, the system updates the catalogue stock and
creates an order in a single database transaction. If any step fails (e.g. stock
update), the whole transaction rolls back, leaving the system consistent. This
is simple and reliable but only works when all changes occur within the same
database or tightly coupled system.

In distributed architectures, especially when the cart, catalogue, and
fulfilment are separate services, ACID is no longer practical across network
boundaries. Instead, systems adopt the BASE approach—Basically Available, Soft
state, Eventual consistency. This accepts that data may be temporarily
inconsistent but will converge over time. For instance, the cart may accept an
order while the catalogue’s inventory update is still “in flight”; for a short
period, the order confirmation and the stock count are out of sync.

To handle this, architects use patterns like SAGAs, which break a large
transaction into a series of local transactions coordinated through events or
messages. In our e-commerce example, the saga starts when the cart service
creates an order. The catalogue service then reserves stock, the payment service
charges the customer, and the fulfilment service prepares shipment. If any step
fails—say payment is declined—compensating actions are triggered: the catalogue
releases stock, the cart updates the order as cancelled, and the saga completes
in a consistent state without requiring a global rollback.

SAGAs allow distributed systems to maintain business consistency under BASE, but
they demand careful design. Developers must account for retries, idempotency,
and compensating logic. The trade-off is clear: while ACID prioritises strict
correctness within a single system, BASE with SAGAs prioritises availability and
resilience at scale, ensuring customers can continue shopping even in the face
of failures or delays in individual services.

#### Asynchronous Communication Topologies

In asynchronous communication, the way producers and consumers are wired
together (the topology) has a big influence on coupling, scalability, and
complexity. Here are the most common topologies, with trade-offs:

1. **Point-to-Point (Queue)**

   A producer sends messages to a queue, and one consumer processes each
   message. For example, the cart service publishes an `OrderPlaced` event to a
   queue, and the fulfilment service consumes it to prepare shipping.

   Benefits:
   - Simple to reason about — one message, one consumer.
   - Natural load balancing if multiple consumers read from the same queue (each
     message is delivered to exactly one).
   - Good for task distribution (e.g. background jobs, order processing).

   Trade-offs:
   - Tight coupling between producer intent and a specific consumer.
   - Harder to extend — if you want multiple services (e.g. fulfilment *and*
     analytics) to react, you need separate queues or message duplication.

2. **Publish-Subscribe (Topic/Broadcast)**

   A producer publishes messages to a topic, and multiple consumers subscribe.
   For example, the catalogue publishes an `ItemUpdated` event, and both cart
   (to refresh its cache) and search (to reindex) consume it independently.

   Benefits:
   - Decouples producers from consumers—the producer doesn’t know or care who is
     listening.
   - Enables fan-out: many consumers can act on the same event for different
     purposes.
   - Encourages domain events and integration without coordination.

   Trade-offs:
   - Consumers must be idempotent and tolerate at-least-once delivery.
   - Order is not always guaranteed, especially with multiple partitions or
     consumers.
   - Debugging is harder when many consumers react in different ways to the same
     event.

3. **Event Streams (Log-Based)**

   Events are stored in an append-only log (e.g. Kafka). Consumers read at their
   own pace, with the ability to replay from any point. For example, cart could
   rebuild its state by replaying all `ItemUpdated` events from catalogue.

   Benefits:
   - Strong support for event sourcing and rebuilding state.
   - Consumers are independent: each maintains its own offset.
   - Good for analytics, auditability, and reprocessing.

   Trade-offs:
   - Requires managing consumer offsets and retention.
   - Higher infrastructure and operational complexity.
   - Events may accumulate in large volumes, requiring careful schema evolution
     and data governance.

4. **Request-Reply over Messaging**

   Instead of direct REST calls, services exchange messages asynchronously with
   correlation ids. For example, the cart sends an `ItemDetailsRequest` event,
   and the catalogue replies with an `ItemDetailsResponse`.

   Benefits:
   - Decouples producer and consumer but still allows query-like interactions.
   - Provides resilience (messages are buffered, no immediate dependency on
     availability).

   Trade-offs:
   - More complex than REST (correlation IDs, temporary reply queues).
   - Response time is less predictable.
   - Easy to misuse and accidentally recreate synchronous coupling over
     messaging.

5. **Choreography (Event-Driven Workflow)**

   Business processes emerge from a sequence of events across services. For
   example, `OrderPlaced` → payment emits `PaymentConfirmed` → fulfilment emits
   `OrderShipped`.

   Benefits:
   - Fully decoupled, no central coordinator.
   - Scales well and supports autonomous teams.

   Trade-offs:
   - Hard to understand and debug — the “workflow” is implicit in event chains.
   - Risk of hidden dependencies or circular event flows.
   - Monitoring and tracing become essential to avoid “spaghetti events.”

6. **Orchestration (Workflow Engine)**

   A central orchestrator (e.g. a workflow engine) sends commands to services,
   often asynchronously. For example, an order service calls payment and
   fulfilment in sequence, tracking the overall saga.

   Benefits:
   - Clear visibility of the process in one place.
   - Easier to handle compensations (e.g. cancel order if payment fails).

   Trade-offs:
   - Introduces a central point of control, which can become a bottleneck.
   - Reduces autonomy compared with choreography.
   - Orchestrator must scale and be highly reliable.
